'''''Picconia azorica''''', locally known as '''pau-branco''', is a species of ''[[Picconia]]'' common to the majority of islands of the [[Portugal|Portuguese]] archipelago of the [[Azores]], where it is [[endemic]]. It can grow to a medium-sized tree, though it is usually found in the form of a shrub. It is threatened by [[habitat loss]].<ref name="iucn status 16 November 2021" />

==Description==
The [[evergreen]] woody plant species is present in all the islands of the Azores, except [[Graciosa]], usually in coastal and medium altitude forests from sea-level up to about {{convert|700|m|abbr=on}} high.<ref>{{cite web |title=Picconia azorica (Tutin) Knobl. |url=https://acores.flora-on.pt/#/1picconia+azorica |publisher=[[Flora-On]] |access-date=18 January 2022}}</ref><ref name="SRAM">{{citation |publisher=SRAM Secretaria Regional do Ambiente e do Mar |year=2008 |title=Plantas Endémicas dos Açores: Guia da Ilha do Faial |page=13 |location=Horta (Azores), Portugal |language=Portuguese}}</ref> Leaves are lanceolate or ovate, opposite and with entire margins. It flowers from March to July, producing small white flowers in axillary clusters.<ref name="Martinsetal39">Martins et al. (2011), p.39</ref> The fleshy fruits are dark blue [[drupes]] about {{convert|1.5|cm|in}} long, similar to olive trees (both plants are in the [[Oleaceae]] family).<ref name=Martinsetal39/><ref name=azores>Azores Flora: [http://www.azorenflora.de/picconia_azorica.html ''Picconia azorica''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180715054221/http://www.azorenflora.de/picconia_azorica.html |date=2018-07-15 }}</ref>

==Status==
The species is very popular in traditional/artesnal carpentry, for furniture construction and religious sanctuary.<ref name=Martinsetal39/>

Since its colonization, the resources of the different islands of the Azores were used to sustain its population. This meant that the forests were also cut-down to support the local economy and day-to-day activities, and other non-endemic species planted to support growing populations, such as the [[Cryptomeria]] (''Cryptomeria japonica'') and the [[Acacia dealbata|Acacia]] (''Acacia dealbata'') (which were quick growing in the habitats of the islands).

[[Overexploitation]] of the wood led to the species becoming almost extinct in some islands.<ref name=Martinsetal39/> It has become a priority for re-population and conservation, listed as endangered on the [[IUCN]] Red List 2004, and Annex II of the Habitats Directive ([[Berne Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats]]), due to habitat degradation, expansion of agricultural land, forestation, competition by invader species and isolation of populations.<ref name=Martinsetal39/>
